target_customer: Families arranging a burial or cremation, with funeral providers as the referral-fee payer
problem: Funeral and cremation prices and reviews were opaque, forcing grieving families to shop around by phone. Halolife offered guided planning and price and review comparison in California.
business_model: Marketplace referral fees from funeral homes

founders.name: Jake Beyer
founders.background_notes: YC page bio lists product manager roles at these companies without dates, so they may postdate Halolife. Education not found.

exit.reason: Founder post-mortem reportedly says lack of traction and funding, and no successful customer acquisition strategy

competitors.name: Willing
competitors.what: YC S15 online platform to compare cost of cremation, burial and ceremonies, same batch as Halolife

technical_complexity.rationale: A directory and planning web app with provider price and review data. The hard part was assembling provider pricing, not engineering.

defensibility.rationale: Provider listings and price data were copyable and a same-batch rival, Willing, addressed the same need. No network effect was established with two founders or fewer.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent copied or bought the idea per sources found. Founder reportedly shut it down near the end of 2016.

market_need_then: Funeral pricing opacity was a recognized consumer complaint and several startups launched in 2015 addressing it, but the founder reportedly found entrenched consumer behavior and no working acquisition channel.

branding.domain_note: Company used halolife.com per the YC page

identity.voice_and_tone: Positioned as caring and transparent per the YC description, no brand voice source found

brand_strength.rationale: No press about the brand itself. Name evokes a halo and afterlife but similar names such as Halo Life trademarks exist, so it was easy to confuse; no evidence it drove traffic.

outcome_analysis: Halolife launched in San Francisco in 2015 as a funeral marketplace, joined YC S15 with two people and raised very little. The founder reportedly wrote that he shut it down toward the end of 2016 because he could not find a customer acquisition strategy for at-need or pre-need buyers and could not secure further funding. A newsletter review also cites ingrained consumer behavior and difficulty serving both sides of the market, and a same-batch rival, Willing, targeted the same problem.
notes: The company site halolife.com returned an HTTP 522 error, so it is treated as unreachable. The Medium post returned 403 to a fetch, so its content is taken from a search summary of it and not opened directly; shutdown timing and reasons therefore rest on that summary plus the Substack write-up. The $120K seed rests on one aggregator (Village.ai), while Seedtable shows no rounds and Crunchbase shows an unspecified pre-seed figure. The summary also mentioned 500 Startups participation but no funding source confirmed it, so it is not recorded as a round. Other funeral startups such as Funeralocity exist but no source dated near the batch was verified, so they are excluded.
